accuracy.reason: The nine objectives are supported with precise operation-level scope, valid real-time ordering, eventual rather than bounded completion, protocol-qualified majority behavior and conditional convergence. No unconditional freshness, merge or availability promise. Broad introductory wording is refined by the subsequent definitions.

evidence.quote: Overlapping operations may be placed in either order, provided the resulting order is valid for one copy. The required order follows completed-before-started relationships, not a globally synchronized timestamp on every request.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state. It does not promise that every conflicting edit survives; the conflict-resolution policy determines the result.

mechanisms.reason: The 10-to-12 split makes the missing information explicit and evaluates answering, waiting, refusing, blocking the write and guessing. The diagrams preserve the confirmed-write-before-read relationship and distinguish running nodes from communication. Majority and reconciliation mechanisms are sufficient for the stated conceptual objectives.

evidence.quote: Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes. The obstacle is missing information, not a particular database product.

coherence.reason: Scope and network failure precede the two formal guarantees; the impossibility example then motivates consistency-preserving and available behaviors, recovery and operation-level selection. Every card objective has an explicit role in the explanation.

evidence.quote: Blocking the original write at A also gives up availability. The conflict exists whichever operation waits.

decisions.reason: Costs are user-visible refusal/delay, stale reads, conflicting changes and possible lost intent. Profile, reservation and offline-edit examples invite operation-specific choices, with explicit recovery obligations and limits on what CAP decides.

evidence.quote: Availability supplies no automatic safe merge. Selecting one conflicting value can lose another user's intent, and cross-record rules require their own protection.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability. It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.

clarity.reason: Distributed system, partition, linearizability, availability, quorum and convergence are explained directly. Overlap versus real-time ordering, error responses versus successful reads, and data agreement versus preserved intent prevent common ambiguous interpretations without unnecessary algorithm detail.

evidence.quote: CAP availability does not mean fast, immediately answered, or a particular uptime percentage. The theorem requires eventual per-request completion and sets no practical response-time target.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria taught in slides 1–2, 5 and 9 and entailed by learner evidence: networked copies, conditional conflict, no universal choose-two menu, living client-reachable partitioned nodes, defined failure behavior without both guarantees, and unavoidable communication risk.

All six criteria explicitly supported by slides 3–4: real-time single-copy order; completed write and valid overlapping orders; distinction from convergence and ACID rules; eventual response without latency bound; refusal/error/indefinite wait not successful availability; uptime as a different measure. The learner does not need outside knowledge.

All three criteria supported. Learner transfers the slide 5 values 10/12 to question values 0/1, correctly identifying B’s old knowledge, required new result, availability versus consistency outcomes and why guessing cannot cover unseen possibilities.

All six criteria taught by slides 6–7 and diagrams: restrict unsafe operations, client delay/failure, safely coordinated pair continues, local stale reads, conflicting accepted writes, and explicit reconciliation that alone cannot guarantee intent or business rules. Majority is explicitly protocol-qualified, not arbitrary vote counting.

All six criteria satisfied by slides 3 and 6–9: conditional propagation/reconciliation convergence; no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes; policy-dependent losses; strict versus stale-tolerant behavior; recovery and user effects; operation/configuration choices separate from normal latency/cost. Learner correctly does not invent a vendor recovery algorithm.

sourceChecks.claim: Gilbert/Lynch paper opened: formal model and impossibility theorem support partition-conditional scope.
Paper section 2.3 explicitly permits lost intercomponent messages; nodes need not crash.
Paper section 2.1 supports single-copy ordering and completed-before-started visibility; slide correctly distinguishes ACID validity.
Paper section 2.2 requires eventual operation termination without a runtime bound; returning refusal is not executing the read.
Paper proof inspected: separate components and a completed remote write create indistinguishable histories for the isolated reader. Diagram matches that barrier.

Raft paper opened, sections 2 and 5 checked: operational communicating majority and protocol safety support the three-node example. The slide does not assert that counting any two replies alone proves safety.
Eric Brewer’s primary article on InfoQ opened, including partition recovery: reconciliation and compensation are separate from simply accepting operations.

AWS read-consistency documentation opened: eventual reads may miss completed writes and per-operation strong-read options exist. General conditional convergence and conflict-policy limits additionally supported by Brewer’s recovery discussion at https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/.
Brewer article supports operation-sensitive partition behavior and recovery; examples are design choices, not claims that CAP alone supplies application invariants or performance predictions.
